youtube.aciklama:
How can an adult with hearing loss prevent and repair breakdowns in conversation? In this lesson we cover anticipatory, facilitative and repair strategies, clear speech, communication partner training and the evidence for computer-based auditory training.

AIHEAR Audiology Academy makes short, clear lessons for audiology students and professionals.

Sources: Tye-Murray, Foundations of Aural Rehabilitation: Children, Adults, and Their Family Members; Erber, Communication Therapy for Hearing-Impaired Adults; Picheny, Durlach and Braida, Speaking clearly for the hard of hearing I, J Speech Hear Res (1985); Henshaw and Ferguson, Efficacy of individual computer-based auditory training for people with hearing loss: a systematic review of the evidence, PLoS One (2013).

This video is for educational purposes and does not replace diagnosis or treatment.

sahneler.alt: Anticipating, facilitating and repairing in adults
cumleler: Hello, and welcome to the AIHEAR Audiology Academy.
In this lesson we will learn strategies an adult with hearing loss can use to prevent and repair breakdowns in conversation.
We will also cover communication partner training and how well computer-based auditory training works.
A communication breakdown is the moment when the listener does not understand a spoken message.
At such moments many people with hearing loss pretend to understand; they nod or smile.
In the short term this avoids embarrassment, but it can lead to misunderstandings and wrong answers.
As breakdowns become more frequent, the person may withdraw from conversation, which turns into a participation restriction.
Communication strategies are the ways a person deliberately uses to reduce and repair breakdowns.
Strategies do not replace the device; even with a well-fitted device, breakdowns happen in noise and at a distance.
Hearing is not the only cause; fast speech, an unfamiliar topic and fatigue also lead to breakdowns.
Grouping strategies into three by when they are used makes them easier to teach.
Anticipatory strategies are used before a conversation, to prepare for likely difficulties.
Facilitative strategies adjust the setting and the speaker during a conversation to make understanding easier.
Repair strategies are used to recover the message when a breakdown occurs.
Many rehabilitation programs, notably Tye-Murray's textbook, are based on this distinction.
The same person may use all three in a single conversation; the aim is to choose the one that best fits the situation.
The first anticipatory strategy is to think ahead about words likely to come up; for example, drug names at the pharmacy.
Before important talks such as a doctor's appointment, questions are written down; knowing the question makes the answer easier to follow.
For an important conversation, a quiet time and place are chosen; a corner table can be requested in a busy restaurant.
When the person mentions the hearing loss at the start, later breakdowns are easier to repair.
Asking for the meeting agenda or the slides in advance also makes the topic easier to follow.
In the clinic, these strategies are planned together around a real situation the person faces.
Facilitative strategies aim to adjust both the setting and the speaker during a conversation.
The person keeps the light behind them, so it falls on the speaker's face and lip movements can be seen.
Moving away from a noise source or turning the better ear toward the speaker also belong to this group.
The speaker can be given a short, polite instruction: could you please speak a little more slowly and face me?
On the phone or at a counter, closed questions narrow the expected answer; for example, is the appointment Tuesday or Wednesday?
Remote microphones, phone captions and speech-to-text apps are also facilitative tools.

ogeler.metin: Could you repeat the last part?

cumleler: Repair strategies are divided into general and specific; requests like pardon or what are general requests.
A general request does not tell the speaker what was missed; the speaker often just repeats the same sentence louder.
In a specific request the person says what was not understood; for example, asking for only the last part to be repeated.
Asking for the sentence to be said in other words prevents the same difficult word from being missed again and again.
Asking for the topic or the key word makes it easier to guess the rest of the sentence.
For critical information such as numbers, addresses and drug names, asking for it in writing is the safest way.
Finally, the person confirms by repeating what they understood; for example, the appointment is at three, right?
The burden of breakdowns is not only on the person with hearing loss; the speaker's style also determines intelligibility.
Clear speech is a speaking style deliberately adopted when talking to someone who has difficulty understanding.
Speech slows a little, short pauses appear between words and sounds are produced more distinctly; shouting is not needed.

cumleler.yazi: In the 1985 study by Picheny and colleagues, listeners with hearing loss understood clear speech markedly better.
cumleler.ses: In the nineteen eighty five study by Picheny and colleagues, listeners with hearing loss understood clear speech markedly better.

cumleler: The average difference measured with nonsense sentences was about 17 percentage points; the bars show an example of this difference.
Some later studies found a smaller benefit; still, clear speech is an easy to teach and powerful tool.
A communication partner is a spouse, child or coworker who regularly talks with the person with hearing loss.
Involving the partner helps reduce the third-party disability we saw in the lesson on psychosocial effects.
In communication partner training, the partner practices clear speech through role play.
Calling the person by name before speaking, being face to face and rephrasing a missed sentence are the core skills.
Goals are set together with the person and the partner; for example, turning off the TV at dinner.
Studies on partner training are growing; early results suggest that satisfaction with communication may improve.

maddeler.metin: The brain adapts to changed input

cumleler: Auditory training is regular listening practice that aims to make better use of sound from a hearing aid or implant.
The basic idea is that the brain can adapt to changed auditory input, in other words neuroplasticity.
Practice follows the steps of detection, discrimination, identification and comprehension from the auditory skills hierarchy lesson.
The stimulus can progress from small units such as syllables and words toward sentences and conversation.
The setting is also made harder step by step: from a quiet room to background noise.
We will look at analytic and synthetic training in detail in the lesson on auditory training for adult implant users.
Computer-based auditory training programs let the person practice at home on a computer or tablet.
Most programs are adaptive: as the person answers correctly, the task gets harder, for example more noise is added.
Feedback after every response lets the person see an error right away.
Programs usually suggest short, frequent sessions over a few weeks; regularity matters more than duration.
Some programs share results with the audiologist, so progress and adherence can be monitored.
In Türkiye, few programs have been adapted and validated in Turkish; check that a program's language and content suit the person.

cumleler.yazi: In 2013, Henshaw and Ferguson systematically reviewed studies of computer-based auditory training in adults.
cumleler.ses: In twenty thirteen, Henshaw and Ferguson systematically reviewed studies of computer-based auditory training in adults.

cumleler: Improvement on the trained task was seen in nearly all studies; people became skilled at the task they practiced.
However, transfer of this gain to untrained speech tests and daily life was small and inconsistent.
Participants' adherence to the programs was generally high, and gains were maintained at short follow-ups.
The authors concluded that the evidence is not yet strong enough to guide clinical decisions with confidence.
So auditory training is more meaningful when planned together with real-life goals and communication strategies.

maddeler.metin: New hearing aid or implant user
Struggling in noise despite verified fit
Motivated and able to practice regularly

cumleler: Auditory training is considered most often for people who are starting to hear new sound through a hearing aid or implant.
People who still struggle to understand in noise although their fitting has been verified are also candidates.
To benefit from home programs, the person needs to be motivated and able to practice regularly.
Before training, the fitting is verified with real-ear measurement; training cannot make an inaudible sound audible.
Auditory training is not offered alone, but together with counseling and communication strategies.
Content is chosen to fit the person's goal; for example, someone aiming to use the phone can practice with phone speech.

sahneler.metin: Teach the patient a specific repair phrase to use instead of 'Pardon?' and try it once in the clinic: 'I missed the time, could you repeat it?'
cumleler: A clinical tip: teach the patient a specific repair phrase to use instead of a general request.
For example, the phrase I missed the time, could you repeat it, tells the speaker right away what is missing.
Try this phrase once in the clinic with a short role play; if a family member is present, give them the speaker's role.
At the next visit, ask in which situation they used it and whether it worked.
Communication strategies are anticipatory before a conversation, facilitative during it and repair strategies after a breakdown.
Specific repair requests that say what was missed are more effective than general requests such as pardon.
The communication partner learns clear speech, and clear speech can markedly improve intelligibility.
Computer-based auditory training improves the trained task, but transfer to daily life is limited.

sahneler.soru: Which is a specific repair request?
secenekler: Could you repeat the last part?
sahneler.aciklama: A specific request tells the speaker _what was missed_.

cumleler.yazi: Test yourself: which of the following is a specific repair strategy?

cumleler: The correct answer is C: could you repeat the last part?
This request tells the speaker what was missed; general requests like pardon do not, and nodding along is bluffing.
